You have a claim for conversion against your roommate and a claim for replevin against the holder of the property. The holder's specific business doesn't have to come into it. Your roommate owed a non-specific debt and used your property to secure it or pay it off. Call it an improper lien securing a debt for another for which you aren't a guarantor or transfer of defective title as the transferor (your roommate) can only pass the title he held in the goods which was none. No cops, just civil claims. Small claims pro se would likely be sufficient.

This is a tough spot because you can do something or do nothing and neither option will be very much fun; i.e. choose between taking the heat or being a doormat. I usually recommend doing something vs. nothing because the doormat option typically comes with a heap of regret if you have an ounce of self-respect. Whichever you decide, good luck!

Thank you for your very informative, and motivational post. I was about to admit defeat and search craigslist for couches and such.

I contacted an attorney friend in DC, as well as a Parole Officer bud of mine and said that this case is completely winnable, but only if I can prove that those possessions are in fact mine, that there was an agreement made to store the stuff there, and that I didn't forfeit my right of ownership by not trying to get them back. They suggested I sit tight in the mean time, and get as much proof as I can over ownership and the such.

My roommate is in another state now, so any action against him (we're talking < $1,000 worth of property) isn't realistic, correct?

And the drug-dealer's last text to me was that any and all communication regarding this matter go through his defense attorney because he doesn't talk "bitch" (classy, eh?). The defense attorney was described by my PO friend as "Not slimy. But good, very good."

So if I can gather up receipts, pictures, notarized letters, etc that prove that these possessions are mine, I should be able to win no matter what kind of bullshit defense he tries to pull, right?

I concur with your friends' advice. Collect as much evidence as you can showing those things belong to you and take it to the Judge; e.g. written statements, pictures, receipts, anything. You might win or you might lose, but standing up for yourself is always worth the effort no matter the result, especially for the minimal cost of a small claims filing.

Also, know that a seasoned attorney's toolkit includes jedi mind tricks to discourage and plant doubt and despair well before the hearing date to knock you off your game. In response to your demand or complaint you will receive a letter stating "you can't win", "stop wasting everyone's time" "your claims are frivolous", etc. Many inexperienced litigants (including new attorneys) will simply give up, and we know this, so don't buy into it or second guess your right to claim your own property.

These ARE the droids you're looking for. Don't let anyone but the Judge tell you otherwise.

Edit: Forgot to mention, you are correct that the out of state thing would be time/cost prohibitive. No shame letting that one go.
